We continue to strengthen protection and access to justice for all women and girls, including through local mechanisms to prevent and respond to gender-based violence, and through greater investment in survivor-centered services. Mr. President, as we move into the next strategic plan, 2026-2029, Nepal welcomes the strategic plan's strategic pathways to progress: advancing women's leadership and decision-making, women's economic empowerment, ending violence against women and girls, and strengthening women's role in peace, security, and humanitarian action as mutually reinforcing pillars of transformative change. Nepal remains firmly committed to advancing the Beijing Declaration Platform for Action, CEDAW, WPS, and 2030 Agenda to ensure gender equality for all women and girls. Let us remind ourselves, equality cannot and should not remain a promise deferred. It must become power, institution, adequate resources for mandate implementation, safety in communities, and opportunities for a sustainable future of all women and Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nepal for his statement. I now give the floor to Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to start by expressing my sincere appreciation to the Executive Director, Shima Bafus, for her opening statement and comprehensive annual report. Japan deeply appreciates UN Women's tireless efforts toward the achievement of SDG 5, as reflected in the annual report and anchored in the Strategic Plan 2022-2025. UN Women's achievement of 61% of indicator targets and good performance for 80-80% of indicators at the development result/output level demonstrates resilient capabilities in the face of global divisions and backlash. Japan remains steadfast in its unwavering support for UN Women as it stands at the forefront of realizing SDG 5. Japan also welcomes The fact that active bilateral dialogue has been maintained through Executive Director's visit to Japan on the occasion of the UN System Chief Executive Board for Coordination this year, following her visit last December— Japan highly values the continued accumulation of substantive dialogue, including the subsequent policy dialogue between UN Women and the Government of Japan, and the bilateral meeting of Parliamentary Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs Eri Harufiya with Deputy Director— Executive Director Kashimari in May of this year. Japan strongly recognizes UN Women as an indispensable partner in advancing gender equality, women's empowerment, and women and peace and security. Japan remains fully committed to maintaining and further strengthening this close partnership going forward. Regarding the ongoing discussions on the proposed merger of UN Women and UNFPA, it is Japan's utmost priority to ensure that the mandates of both entities are preserved, regardless of which option is ultimately pursued. Japan also strongly urges that the process be conducted with full transparency. Mr. President, Japan, as an Executive Board member, will continue to work closely with UN Women in further advancing its mandate. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Korea for his statement— sorry, Japan. My apologies. Japan for his statement. And I give the floor to Croatia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Executive Director, Excellencies, Croatia thanks the Executive Director for her report and presentation. We also express our sincere appreciation to the staff of UN Women for their dedication and hard work in a challenging global context. Distinguished colleagues, no country has achieved gender equality. This sentence is written on the second page of the report of the Executive Director. We should not take lightly that this is a sentence we still must write in 2026. This is by no means a reason to concede defeat, but the weight of those words should stay with us. The report confirms the scale of the challenges upon us, but it also confirms the value of a strong, effective, and well-resourced UN Women. At a moment of disruption, we must match political commitments with financing and and sustained support. And Croatia welcomes the tangible results achieved under the strategic plan, including the scaling up of UN Women's work on peace, security, and humanitarian action. The impact of conflict on women and girls is evident across many contexts. Yet women remain underrepresented in peace processes, as well as reconstruction efforts. And Croatia therefore strongly supports UN Women's continued presence in crisis settings. From our own experience, Croatia can attest to the positive role women play in reconciliation, accountability, the search for the missing persons, and the rebuilding of the social fabric after conflict. Madam President, gender equality should be a system-wide effort. We should like to underline the important work of the Peacebuilding Commission and the Peacebuilding Fund, whose gender-responsive programmes have delivered tangible results in the most fragile contexts. Croatia has also consistently advocated within the Peacebuilding Commission for a stronger focus on women's economic empowerment as an important component of sustaining peace. Croatia remains committed to cooperation with UN Women, including through the "She Demines" project in Ukraine, which brings together mine action, recovery and women's leadership. Finally, as discussions on UN Aid Reform continue, Member States need clear and timely information to take decisions that strengthen, not weaken the UN gender equality architecture. We welcome committed efforts to improve governance, accountability, transparency, and results-based delivery. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of Croatia for his comments. I now give the floor to South Africa.

Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank the Executive Director for for her report, and South Africa commends UN Women's resolve and commitment to effectively implement its strategic plan. The most striking elements of the report is the successful advancing of the triple mandate of the UN— of UN Women while making gains on the achievement of the SDGs. South Africa is particularly pleased with the progress made in women's economic empowerment, especially the normative efforts in championing gender-responsive care systems. These results are a validation of the strategic approach of UN Women, as well as its importance towards the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals. We remain concerned about the continued prevalence of gender-based violence and recognize the continuous efforts of UN Women in support of whole-of-society approaches to combat this scourge. Continued support in the development of prevention action plans, survivor-centered services, and partnerships with key stakeholders is deeply appreciated and greatly encouraged. Mr. President, the proliferation of conflicts and impact on civilians has the greatest impact on women and girls, and these groups often remain overlooked in the potential value they offer under the Women, Peace and Security Agenda. Despite these and other ongoing challenges, the results reported today are a testament to the inherent value of the multilateral processes and constructive partnerships. The triple mandate of UN Women is serving its objective. This formula is working. In conclusion, We recommit our continuous support for the strategic direction of UN Women. The report on the implementation of the Strategic Plan confirms sustained progress. Whilst we may not be observing this at the pace which we have targeted, we should not diminish this progress nor change our course. Our commitment to UN Women as a valued partner remains steadfast, and we look forward to the next strategic plan in the final push towards 2030. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa for his remarks. I now give the floor to the Russian Federation.

Thank you, Mr. President. We thank the Executive Director of UN Women, Sima Bahus, for her presentation of the report. At this challenging time for the United Nations, the Russian Federation supports the organization's efforts to achieve equality between women and men. Our country, which enshrined equality between women and men in the Constitution over 100 years ago, has traditionally attached particular importance to this agenda item and the associated entity. The entity's activities should be focused on implementing its unique trickle mandate and not go beyond the limits of that mandate. UN Women must also act exclusively at the request and with the consent of member states. The unauthorized expansion of its activities, especially in the human rights area, not only dilutes the important work of the entity in improving the status of women but also undermines trust in it from— on the part of developing countries for whom socioeconomic issues are particularly acute. Genuine improvement in the status of women is achieved not by promoting controversial concepts, but by providing genuine assistance for women's professional development, support for mothers and families, and ensuring social protection and equal access to economic opportunities and education. Noting the important role of UN Women in supporting women's organizations on the ground, We call on it to avoid going beyond the scope of engagement agreed with states and to promote dialogue between governments and the non-governmental sector. UN bodies cannot support the confrontational activity of externally sponsored civil society organizations. The Russian Federation is committed to a constructive dialogue within the Executive Board. We believe that UN Women must act as an impartial body whose sole task is to improve the status of women worldwide. To this end, it is important that it distance itself from political bias, avoid double standards, and take the interests and positions of all states into account equally. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation, Federation. And I'll give the floor to New Zealand. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President and Madam Executive Director. New Zealand commends UN Women for its continued leadership in advancing gender equality and the empowerment of all all women and girls in an increasingly complex global environment. We meet at a time when progress on gender equality is under significant pressure. Conflict, climate change, and economic instability are exacerbating inequalities and reinforcing barriers to women's full participation in society. In this context, UN Women's triple mandate is more important than ever. We particularly welcome UN Women's continued focus on reaching those most at risk, including in fragile and crisis-affected settings, and its emphasis on strengthening national systems, supporting women's organizations and movements, and locally-led approaches. New Zealand places particular importance on UN Women's engagement in our Pacific region. Women and girls in the Pacific face disproportionate challenges, including climate-related risks, economic vulnerability, the lowest levels of women's political representation globally and among the highest rates of gender-based violence. We welcome UN Women's continued work to support women's leadership, resilience, and economic participation in Pacific Island countries. Turning to the broader context, New Zealand strongly supports the Secretary-General's UN80 initiative. The UN development system must be more focused, more efficient, and better coordinated particularly at the country level, including through the retention of strong in-country technical capability. As we consider the reform agenda ahead, New Zealand recognises that a range of options are being advanced to strengthen the effectiveness and coherence of the system. It is important that these are assessed holistically, and we underline the important role of this Board in providing strategic guidance and driving timely informed decisions. Given the urgency of the challenges we face, we should move beyond analysis and towards clear conclusions and direction so that reforms can be implemented without delay. Mr. President, Executive Director, New Zealand remains concerned about the challenging funding environment facing UN Women. Core, predictable, and flexible funding is essential to enable UN Women to effectively to advance gender equality and women's rights, maintain its normative leadership, strengthen systems and institutions, and respond to emerging needs. We encourage all partners to support UN Women through flexible contributions and to ensure resources are directed toward areas where they can deliver lasting impacts for all women and girls. In closing, New Zealand reaffirms its strong support for UN Women and its vital role in advancing gender equality globally. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of New Zealand for his remarks. I now give the floor to Switzerland.

Monsieur le Président, Madame la Directrice, President, Madame Executive Director, Switzerland commends UN Women for its accomplishment in the context of the Strategic 2030 Plan 2022-2025. Despite an exceptionally difficult context, UN Women has delivered excellent results in implementing its triple mandate. Switzerland welcomes the fact that UN Women remains a reliable and agile partner, including in crisis situations. Allow me to share 3 observations. First, UN Women reaffirms its central role in strengthening women's voices, leadership, and agency by achieving 115% of of its targets in this area for the period. We particularly commend UN Women's efforts to strengthen localization through the provision of high-quality and flexible funding to local women's organizations and feminist movements. Second, significant global challenges in gender equality remain. Progress is still too slow. At the current pace, SDG 5 will not be achieved by 2030. This finding comes at a time when voluntary contributions to UN Women and global funding for gender equality are declining. In this context, UN Women plays an essential role in accelerating progress. Switzerland remains committed to supporting UN Women through predictable, flexible, and multi-year financing and calls on all Member States to do the same. Third, we recognize the significant progress made by UN Women in the context of the United Nations Development System reform initiated in 2018. We call on UN Women to actively contribute to the implementation of the UN80 Initiative and accelerate the necessary reforms. Switzerland invites UN Women to continue strengthening system-wide coherence through shared services, joint programs, and pooled funding mechanisms, particularly with UNFPA. Reform efforts must translate into tangible efficiency gains at the country level, and we encourage UN Women to establish indicators to measure this progress. Finally, Switzerland reaffirms its strong support for UN Women's triple mandate: normative leadership on the rights of all women and girls, coordination and accountability of the collective action of the United Nations system in favor of gender equality, and the operational implementation of women's empowerment. Supporting and protecting this mandate has never been more important than it is today. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of Switzerland for his statement, and I'll give the floor to Colombia.

Thank you, President. Colombia is grateful to Madam Executive Director and to her team for the report. We recognize the sustained leadership of all of you at UN Women, and we recognize your work in promoting gender equality, the empowerment of women and girls, in preventing and responding to all forms of gender-based violence. We especially appreciate the results achieved by the United Nations Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women. These results show that prevention is most effective when women's leadership is supported, social norms can be transformed, and community capacity is strengthened. Columbia also welcomes the fact that 74,300 women and girls have accessed specialized services supported by the Fund's partners. This is the, uh, highest figure in the strategic plan, uh, for the period through 2025. These developments show the value of integrated, sustained, and survivor-centered approaches, and also the importance of strengthening referral pathways, institutional capacity, efficiency and quality standards. We also recognize UN Women's management efforts to consolidate priorities, streamline indicators, and strengthen program— programmatic coherence. The Executive Board also has a central responsibility. We must accompany efforts aimed at efficiency, simplification, and institutional coherence without reducing the substantive scope and programmatic orientation of UN Women. Efficiency cannot be understood as an administrative exercise. It must serve to enhance the entity's capacity to address the priorities of women and girls, especially in those contexts of greatest exclusion, violence, and inequality. It is incumbent upon this board to ensure that management decisions preserve the UN Women's normative ambition, programmatic presence and capacity for transformation. But this cannot be achieved without the predictability and sustainability of resources. We must strengthen the core funding of UN Women. Flexible funding is crucial to ensuring that all women, and especially women facing multiple and intersectional forms of discrimination, continue to to lead conservation actions, community resilience, and sustainable development. We agree with the Executive Director that these commitments must translate into strengthened collective capacity to deliver stepped-up and effective enhancement for women and girls. Thank you, the distinguished representative of Colombia, for his statement.
I now give the floor to China. Uganda has the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President, Executive Director, distinguished members of the board, fellow delegates. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the delegation of Uganda. We wish to thank the President of the board and Executive Director for their leadership and comprehensive updates shared. We commend UN Women for the significant and measurable results it has delivered across the globe, including in the African region. UN Women has been a vital partner in advancing gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls, including in the areas of political participation, economic empowerment, elimination of violence against women and girls, and the promotion of women's leadership in peace and security. These achievements have been hard-won, often under complex and resource constraints.— circumstances. We recognize the urgent need to accelerate progress on SDG 5, which remains foundational to achieve the full 2030 Agenda justice. We welcome the updates on the strategic plan with sharpened focus, strong regional engagement, and commitment to partnership with governments and women-led organizations. We stress the need for sustainable, predictable financing and encourage continued efforts to expand and diversify resource mobilization. We welcome the UN Women's leadership in advancing system-wide reforms through the UN 80 reform process, and we stress the need for timely, transparent, and comprehensive assessments to enable member states to engage meaningfully in the process. Reform efforts must strengthen rather than dilute the capacity of UN Women to deliver on its mandate and support member states in achieving gender equality and empowerment of all women and girls. As I conclude, equality is not just a right, It is a pathway to peace, resilience, and progress. Uganda stands ready to work in partnership to realize this vision for all women and girls. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of Uganda for his statement. I now give the floor to the United Kingdom.

Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of the United Kingdom, I thank the Executive Director for her briefing and continued leadership alongside the UN Women staff operating in challenging and complex circumstances. The United Kingdom remains steadfast in its commitment to gender equality and to the rights, safety, and agency agency of all women and girls. Tackling violence against women and girls is at the heart of UK foreign policy, and we remain fully committed to UN Women's mandate. We welcome the Executive Director's final report on the Strategic Plan 2022-2025 and UN Women's demonstratable results at scale. Yet the picture is clear: progress has been real, but nowhere near fast enough. No country has achieved gender equality. The world is off track to meet SDG 5 by 2030. Violence against women and girls remains an international emergency. Participation in work and public life remains unequal, and unpaid care continues to fall disproportionately on women. These are not only indicators but measures of power, opportunity, and security. Women and girls want to live free from violence, contribute equally to their economies and societies, and shape decisions that affect their lives. The international system must stand with them, including against rollback of hard-won rights. We value UN Women's work to tackle these challenges, including our partnership on the Gender Justice Platform and the International Alliance on Preventing Sexual Violence in Conflict. Conflict alongside our collaboration on the Women, Peace and Security Agenda. The UN Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women also remains an important instrument for supporting community-level responses, particularly in conflict and humanitarian settings. Together, these efforts help advance women's meaningful participation, strengthen survivor-centered accountability, and improve the international response to conflict-related sexual violence. Looking ahead, and as a longstanding partner, we look to UN Women to protect and advance gender equality norms and standards, gender mainstreaming, system coherence, and support to resident coordinators and UN development system reform. Strong accountability is essential. The strategic plan and results framework must help sharpen priorities, support learning, and monitor impact as we crucially approach 2030. 2030. Progress on risk management, financial oversight, and safeguarding must continue with consistent implementation across country offices. Equally, strong controls must persist in the approach to protect— to protecting against sexual exploitation, abuse, and harassment. The UK will remain a constructive partner, ambitious of reform, clear on mandates, focused on accountability, and committed to results for women and girls. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom for her statement and I'll give the floor to China.

Chair, China thanks Executive Director Bajous for the briefing and commends UN Women for the efforts in advancing the implementation of the previous strategic plan. The current challenges confronting the global cause of women's empowerment further underscore the importance of UN Women. I would like to make 4 points. First, UN Women should lead through action. The Strategic Plan 2026-2029 of UN Women provides the framework and strategic blueprint for advancing gender equality over the next 4 years. Only by working together with determination and resolve, and by translating the plan's 4 strategic Strategic Pathways and the 3 Transformative Goals into concrete results, can we effectively accelerate progress towards achieving the gender equality targets of the 2030 Agenda. Second, UN Women should prioritize key areas. Gender issues are not just about matters of human rights, but also matters of development. Survival and development provide the foundation for women's empowerment. We hope that the UN Women will continue to be development-oriented, invest more resources and focus on areas such as poverty alleviation, education, health, employment, and social protection for women, thereby laying a solid foundation for women's comprehensive development. Third, UN Women should embrace changes. Advancing the cause of women requires us to uphold fundamental principles while fostering innovation. We support UN Women in continuing to participate in the UN 8 Initiative while focusing Based on its triple mandate, UN Women should further optimize its organizational effectiveness, better leverage its competitive advantages, and strengthen coordination and collaboration with the UNFPA and UNICEF and other agencies so as to better deliver results. Fourth, UN Women should better mobilize funding. Currently, the funding gap for the global cause of women's development continues to widen, seriously hindering progress towards the gender equality targets, particularly in developing countries. We call on all parties to increase their support for UN Women's core budget and development programs. We also hope that UN Women can effectively diversify its funding sources and fundraising strategy, and also enhance the transparency, effectiveness, and efficiency of fund utilization. China will fulfill its commitment to contribute $10 million to UN Women over the next 5 years, bilateral exchanges and cooperation, and we are ready to work with all parties to translate the consensus reached in the Global Leaders Meeting on Women last October into concrete actions and accelerate the new progress for women's all-round development. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of China for his statement. I now give the floor to Lesotho. Lesotho, you have the floor.

Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, distinguished members of the Executive Board, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Kingdom of Lesotho is honored to address the annual session of the UN Women Executive Board under Agenda Item 2. We thank the Executive Director for the comprehensive annual report which demonstrates UN Women's continued leadership in advancing gender equality, strengthening multilateral cooperation, and supporting member states to accelerate the implementation of Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, the 23rd Agenda, and commitments under UNAET. The Kingdom of Lesotho welcomes the strong results achieved in 2025, particularly in women's economic empowerment, ending gender-based violence, advancing women's leadership in peace and governance, and strengthening gender-responsive financing. We commend UN Women for its expanded support to countries in crisis and for its efforts to ensure that humanitarian responses remain gender-responsive and grounded in the lived realities of women and girls. As a committed Executive Board member For the 2026-2028 term, the Kingdom of Lesotho reaffirms its dedication to working collaboratively with all Member States to ensure that UN Women is well-resourced, strategically positioned, and institutionally strengthened to deliver on its mandate. We underscore the importance of predictable, flexible, and sustainable financing, which remains essential for achieving transformative results at scale. At the national level, Lesotho continues to advance gender equality through strengthened social protection systems, expanded digital inclusion initiatives, and renewed efforts to prevent and respond to gender-based violence. We are deepening partnerships with UN Women to enhance institutional capacity capacity, accelerate implementation of the African Gender and Development Index, and support women's leadership across all sectors of society. The Kingdom of Lesotho also emphasizes that the UN 80 Initiative must reinforce multilateralism and ensure that gender equality remains central to global development, peace, and security efforts. We welcome UN Women's role in the shaping in shaping this agenda and call for continued support to least developed countries, where structural inequalities remain profound and where investment in women and girls yields the highest returns. Mr. President, the Kingdom of Lesotho emphasizes the Executive Director's commitment to transparency, accountability, and results-based management.
I thank the distinguished delegate of Lesotho for his comments. I now give the floor to Morocco.

Merci, Monsieur le Président. Thank you, President. The Kingdom of Morocco would like to begin by expressing its gratitude to the Executive Director of UN Women for the presentation of the annual report, which reflects remarkable work accomplished under particularly demanding conditions. Morocco also wishes to extend its warm congratulations to the President of the Executive Board, as well as to the entire Bureau, for their sustained efforts in the service of a mandate that has never been more crucial. President, Morocco fully aligns itself with the priorities advanced by UN Women and is a committed partner in their implementation. Equality between men and women, the empowerment of women and girls, and their full and effective participation in economic, political, and social life constitute key pillars of the Kingdom's national policy under the leadership of His Majesty King Mohammed VI. At the legislative and institutional levels, Morocco continued in 2026 to strengthen its legal framework in favor of women's rights by pursuing ongoing reforms in the areas of protection against violence, access to justice, and economic empowerment. With regard to political representation, Morocco is continuing its efforts to increase women's participation in elected bodies and positions of responsibility through quota mechanisms and proactive parity policies. The pioneering study conducted by Morocco and referenced in the Executive Director's report which estimated that unpaid domestic work represents 26% of national GDP, illustrates the data-driven approach that now guides public policy development in Morocco, an approach that recognizes and gives due appreciation to women's invisible contribution to the economy. Regarding the issue of a potential merger between UN Women and UNFPA, Morocco has taken note of the strategic evaluation of April 2026, as well as the document on legal implications presented by the Office of Legal Affairs. Morocco reaffirms its commitment to full respect for the distinct and complementary mandates of the two organizations. To predictable and sustainable financing can measure it with their ambitions. Action must remain strong, targeted, and measurable for the benefit of recipient populations. Morocco renews its affirm support for UN Women and its Strategic Plan 2026-2029 and commits to remaining an active, contributing, constructive partner in achieving gender empowerment, gender equality, and the empowerment of women and girls. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Morocco for his statement. I now give the floor to Spain.

Spain thanks the Executive Director and the entire UN Women team for presenting this annual report, and above all, we thank them for their leadership at a particularly complex time for the multilateral system and for the global gender equality agenda, at a time when women's rights are once again being questioned and renegotiated. And in this context, UN Women represents one of the main institutional guarantees in terms of safeguarding the progress made and further promoting transformation still pending. Spain has a firm commitment to feminist cooperation on foreign policy. This is grounded in the universality and indivisibility of human rights and the conviction that gender equality is not just a fundamental right, but a necessary condition for achieving sustainable development, lasting peace, and more robust and inclusive democracies. This is why Spain considers UN Women to be a key strategic partner, and we are particularly gratified to have recently signed a new strategic partnership framework for the period 2026 through 2029. In it, we reaffirm our shared priorities and our willingness to further strengthen this historic partnership. This new framework reflects our common commitment to three priority areas. Firstly, the economic empowerment of women through the promotion of care policies, financing, and budgets with a gender perspective. Secondly, the elimination of all forms of violence against women and girls. This includes technology-facilitated violence. And thirdly, promoting women's leadership and the effective participation of women at all levels of decision-making, including advancing the Women, Peace and Security Agenda and supporting feminist and women's organizations as essential agents of change. Spain also wishes to highlight the importance of the recent conference on feminist foreign policy held in Madrid. This brought together governments, international organizations, civil society, and feminist leaders from all different regions of the world. The conference highlighted that feminist approaches are not just a matter of principle, but also of effectiveness. This commitment is reflected also in our financial support to the organization. Just 3 years, Spain has more than increased its contribution to UN Women's core resources by 6-fold. We reiterate the importance of predictable, flexible, and quality funding to enable UN Women to effectively fulfill its normative coordination and operational mandates. For this reason, Spain has increased the level of multi-year commitments to the agency in order to increase the predictability of the lines of work. Spain thus reaffirms its full support for UN Women, and we look forward to continuing to work together to advance the rights, leadership, and empowerment of all women and girls. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Spain for his comments, and I'll give the floor to UAE.

Madam Executive Director, colleagues, I thank you for your statements, and Executive Director Bahous for presenting the final report on the Implementation of the UN Women Strategic Plan 2022-2025. The report underscores that the progress toward gender equality remains fragile and cannot be assumed. Despite persistent challenges, it shows that targeted investments, effective partnerships, and sustained political commitment can yield meaningful results— even in a complex global environment. The implementation of this strategic plan offers clear guidance for the future. First, amid fiscal constraints and competing priorities, we must expand blended financing mechanisms, mobilize private capital through targeted incentives, and deepen collaboration with international financial institutions to scale proven high-impact programs that deliver measurable outcomes for women and girls. Second, closing gaps for women and girls in conflict and crisis settings require operationalizing the humanitarian-development-peace nexus through joint programming, ensuring that dedicated funding for women-led organizations and systematically integrating women's leadership and participation in peace processes, recovery planning, and reconstruction efforts. Third, as emerging technologies evolve, we must establish clear policy framework to prevent and respond to technology-facilitated violence, invest in the digital literacy and STEM education for women and girls, and expand equitable access access to digital infrastructure so they can safely and fully benefit from innovation. Looking ahead to Strategic Plan 2026-2029, the UAE encourages a continued focus on impact and efficiency. The next strategic plan should leverage UN Women's comparative advantages, strengthen its coordination role across the UN system, and prioritize scalable solutions to accelerate progress toward the 2030 Agenda. The UAE remains a committed partner to the UN Women and looks forward to constructive engagements with Board members throughout this session. And I thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of United Arab Emirates. I now give the floor to Australia.

Thank you, President. Gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls remain urgent global priorities. Australia is firmly committed to this agenda, recognizing the clear and well-established benefits. Advancing gender equality reduces poverty and conflict, strengthens social cohesion and well-being, unlocks economic growth, and enhances prosperity for current and future generations. In this context, we continue to see the enduring importance of UN Women's triple mandate— its normative role, its coordination across the UN system, and its programming work on the ground. Together, these functions are essential to driving systemic change and delivering tangible outcomes for women and girls everywhere. Australia continues to support efforts to advance meaningful reform through the UN80 Initiative. We support bold change that preserves what matters most and ensures the system is equipped for future challenges. At the same time, the proposed merger of UN Women and UNFPA must be assessed on its merits, based on clear evidence of its capacity to strengthen delivery and impact while fully preserving agreed mandates. We again seek assurance that those mandates will be safeguarded through any reform process and underscore the important role of the executive boards in reviewing merger proposals. While we are prepared to consider the merits of a merger, alternate reform options should also be fully examined. We welcome the joint work underway to develop options for member states' consideration, and encourage these to be shared at the earliest opportunity. As a long-standing partner of UN Women, we remain committed to reforms that protect its critical functions and mandates, preserve service delivery, and strengthen the UN system's capacity for delivering for women and girls. UN Women's work to build resilience to disasters, reduce discrimination, and support survivors of violence, including in our region, the Indo-Pacific, has made a meaningful difference, and we would like to see it continue. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia for her statement. I now give the floor to Noe. My updated list of speakers has Libya, Brazil, Cuba, and Mexico. Norway, you have the floor.

Thanks a lot, President, and dear colleagues. Norway wishes to thank UN Women for its tireless efforts to promote and to protect women's rights and gender equality. And Madam Executive Director Sima, thanks a lot for your briefing and for the annual report presented to us today, and to your entire leadership here and to all staff working 24/7 across the globe to protect women's rights. Allow me to highlight 3 quick points. First, women's rights and gender equality remains a top priority in Norway's foreign and development policy, both politically and of course financially. This is why we are maintaining a high level of core support to the UN Women. Second, we welcome the very robust results documented in the annual report. We would, however, encourage a stronger analysis on how outputs contribute to systemic change, including impacts on target groups. And given the continued, continued funding pressures, we are worried about how financial constraints potentially also can affect the UN Women's performance and the UN system-wide efforts towards gender equality. Could you share insights into the consequences of persistent gaps in capacity and financing for gender equality across the UN system, and what can be done to improve this situation? We'd welcome reflections on that. We welcome how the UN Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women strengthens local women's organizations, as you emphasized in your briefing, Zima. Could you also then share more information about UN Women's work towards supporting local women's organizations? And are different mechanisms, including the UN Trust Fund and the Women, Peace and Humanitarian Fund, complementary at country level. Third and finally, when rights and democracy are weakened, the risk of conflict and crisis increases. And we know it is the poorest and the most vulnerable amongst us who suffer the most when the ideological tide is turning and funding is cut. Strengthening the UN as a key arena for developing and defending norms on gender equality is therefore a top priority for Norway. We want a UN that is fit for purpose and that delivers measurable impact for people on the ground. This is why Norway firmly supports the Secretary-General's UN reform initiative generally. When it comes to the suggested merger, we will come back to that in the afternoon, but just stress here, we need safeguards and we need to protect and preserve the distinct mandate of UN Women. Thanks a lot.
I thank the distinguished representative of Norway for his statement. I'll now give the floor to Libya. Libya have the floor.

Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, the State of Libya wishes to express its appreciation for the efforts undertaken by UN Women in the implementation of its mandate and to thank the Executive Secretary for the comprehensive reports presented during this session, particularly those related to the implementation of the strategic plan, as well as the functions of evaluation, internal audit, and ethics. Libya reaffirms its continued support for the work of the entity in advancing the rights and empowerment of women in a manner consistent with the priorities of member states and their national specificities. Libya has carefully reviewed the reports submitted on offsite functions and underscores the importance of strengthening transparency and accountability within the system, ensuring the independence of these essential functions and providing them with the necessary resources. Libya also commends the progress achieved in improving the quality of evaluations and stresses the need to draw upon their findings to guide policies and programs, thereby enhancing efficiency and effectiveness at the national level. With regard to efforts to support women and girls, Libya reaffirms its its firm commitment to ensuring their full rights and enhancing their participation across all sectors, in line with national priorities and the country's broader trajectory towards women's empowerment. In this context, Libya highlights the important role played by the Ministry of Women's Affairs in formulating policies and programs aimed at advancing the status of women and girls, strengthening their participation in public life, and ensuring equal access to services and opportunities. Libya emphasizes that investing in the capacities of women and girls constitutes constitutes a fundamental pillar for achieving sustainable development and promoting societal stability. Libya welcomes the progress made in the implementation of the United Nations Development System reform and underscores the importance of enhancing inter-agency coordination, improving operational efficiency, and developing joint working mechanisms that contribute to achieving tangible results at the national level. Libya stresses that these reforms must be grounded in respect for national priorities and development needs while taking into account the cultural and social specificities of member states. Regarding the ongoing discussions on structural reform initiatives, Libya underscores the importance of ensuring that such discussions are inclusive and transparent and that they are based on complete information and thorough analysis, including assessments of potential impacts on country programs, existing mandates, and technical capacities. Libya stresses the need to preserve the mandates of entities as established by UN bodies and to ensure the programs responding to national priorities remain unaffected. Libya reaffirms its commitment to constructive cooperation with the Executive Board and UN Women and to working collectively to advance the rights and empowerment of women in full respect for the cultural and social values of member states in a manner that contributes to sustainable development for all. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished delegate of Libya for his statement. I now give the floor to Brazil.

Mr. President, Madam Executive Director, distinguished Board Members and observers, Brazil values its close partnership with UN Women and remains firmly committed to strengthening our cooperation. Regarding the Annual Report for 2025, Brazil considers it a comprehensive and balanced assessment of the entity's work. The report demonstrates that UN Women successfully concluded an implementation cycle —of its strategic plan, achieving positive overall performance and delivering significant progress across its three pillars of work. Brazil welcomes the report reference to the country as an example of positive results in the areas of human rights and nondiscrimination. We are committed to institutionalizing intersectional approaches in gender equality policies, making them more responsive, to the specific needs of African descendant and indigenous women. We remain committed to strengthening public policies that promote equality, inclusion, and social justice. Although the annual report does not explicitly refer to South-South and triangular cooperation, several of the initiatives highlighted, such as the Tlatelolco Commitment, refer to valuable collaboration among developing countries. I take this opportunity to highlight some important initiatives undertaken in 2025 within the framework of Brazil's cooperation with UN Women. Under the program Pathways to Equality, the regional dimensions— the regional dimension was expanded with a focus on generating and disseminating knowledge to advance the economic empowerment of rural women in Latin America and the Caribbean. At the institutional level, important progress was made in mainstreaming gender into Brazil's international development cooperation. Another important development was the establishment of a partnership among the Brazilian— the Brazilian Agency for Cooperation, UN Women, and Brazil's Ministry of Development and Social Assistance to promote regional dialogue on care policies. We reaffirm the strategic importance of our partnership with UN Women in promoting gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls, fostering the exchange of best practices and strengthening capacities among countries. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Brazil for her comments. I now give the floor to Cuba.

President, esteemed Sima Bahus, we recognize the indispensable work of UN Women and we support the calls to guarantee sufficient, flexible, and predictable funding to enable the entity to fully complete its mandate in the furtherance of gender equality and women's empowerment. For Cuba, the advancement of women is not a future aspiration or an abstract concept. It is a reality that we have built up over decades with political will and social justice, and the results are tangible. Cuban women actively participate in all areas of our national life. Women represent a considerable majority among professionals in the areas of health, education, science, and the legal sector. Women represent more than half of parliamentary constituencies, and they enjoy firm legal footing through the Constitution, the Family Code, and the Comprehensive Strategy for Preventing and Tackling Gender Violence, including domestic violence. Cuba was the first country to sign and the second country to ratify CEDAW. With this record in defense of the advancement of women, Cuba has decided to to present the candidacy of Dr. Yamila González Ferrer for reelection as an expert on CEDAW, and we would be grateful for the support of member states on the coming 26th of June. President, women and girls in Cuba are suffering today as they have never suffered before. They are suffering the devastating impacts of the United States economic, commercial, and financial blockade, the oil stranglehold, and secondary sanctions against those who have decided to trade with Cuba. More than 32,000 pregnant mothers— women today face greater risk due to the lack of medical supplies and also due to prolonged blackouts that prevent follow-up diagnostics. Cuban women today face a lack of transportation, a lack of electricity, gas, and water services due to fuel shortages. Cuban mothers live with the anguish of continuous power cuts. These are a hindrance to daily life and to the normal functioning of hospitals, neonatal wards, and intensive care units, and also surgical units where their children receive care. These are not mere statistics. The blockade exists, it causes harm, and on many occasions it kills. It amounts to the collective punishment of an entire people and its effects fall disproportionately upon women and girls. Despite these enormous challenges, Cuba will rise up again as it has done so many times. We will not give up on our commitment to gender equality, social justice, and the empowerment of women. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba for her statement. I now give the floor to Mexico.

Muchas gracias. Thank you very much, President. Distinguished Executive Director, colleagues, members, observers. Allow me to begin by pointing out that Mexico recognizes UN Women as the central actor in the multilateral system for converting global commitments in the area of gender equality into concrete public policies, such as, for instance, those derived from the Commission on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women, CEDAW, the Beijing Platform, and the Women, Peace and Security Agenda. The report we are reviewing today is particularly important. It concludes the cycle for the UN Women Strategic Plan 2022-2025. It highlights important progress in a global context that is adverse, that includes multiple crises, setbacks, and growing opposition to gender equality. And we note with great concern that there is a— there's still a global structural lag. No country has achieved gender equality. Women only have 64% of the rights that men enjoy. And under the current trajectory, SDG 5 will not be achieved by 2030, and this was an indispensable condition for sustainable development. The gaps that we find to be particularly critical are found in the areas of labor participation, unpaid care work, political representation, and gender-based violence. And we recognize that despite this challenging context, UN Women has been able to achieve results on a global scale, including strengthening legal frameworks, adoptioning— adopting equality laws and policies, and enabling access to services and resources for more than 14 million women. Against this backdrop, Mexico emphasizes the need to speed up action to strengthen financing and avoid regulatory regression. As regards our At the national level, Mexico has its priorities aligned with the actions reported in the report, especially promoting comprehensive care systems. We have a national progressive care system which we continue to strengthen, and we think that this is the best vehicle to achieve substantive equality and for the full enjoyment of women's rights. Secondly, combating all forms of violence against women and girls, including digital violence, and promoting women's participation in decision-making. We hope that we will be laying the groundwork for strengthening UN Women, both in terms of its mandate and in terms of its actions on the ground. We hope that member states will unite around the priority of equipping UN Women with the resources that it needs in order to continue bringing services to millions of women and girls, and in contributing to the construction of a world where substantive equality is a reality for all people. Mexico. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished delegate of Mexico for her comments. We have had the last speaker on my list. I'll now invite the Secretariat for a few more remarks. May I now invite the Deputy Executive Director, Executive Director, Madam— okay, Deputy Executive Director, Chrissy Mahdi, for the remarks. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Mr. President, and I really would like to start by just thanking all the delegations for your, first of all, insightful comments, but most importantly, especially for your strong support for UN Women. It's been really heartwarming to listen to you this morning, how you have emphasized our mandate, the criticality of our triple mandate, how you have emphasized the challenging context that is there and the importance of the political commitment, how you have also noted the improvements that UN Women has made as an organization on how we are working, on our effectiveness, on our efficiency, and how you have highlighted the results that we have been able to achieve. At the same time, your strong call for predictable and flexible funding, core funding for the organization, has been really critical. So I really want to thank you on behalf of all of us for that very strong expression of support for our work until now and moving forward. There are a couple of specific questions and I would like to— I know we are running out of time soon, but I will try to respond concisely to some of the specific questions that have been raised and my colleague Narazai will then complement, and if you need further details afterwards, we'll be of course available. In the group statement that was presented by Luxembourg, there were questions, for example, on sustainability, how we are actually ensuring the sustainability moving from one strategic plan to the next one. And just very concretely tell you, 80% of the indicators of the strategic plan were adopted from the previous strategic plan. This helps us to really build on a multi-accumulative results across moving from one strategic plan cycle to another. Also, the— we've embedded sustainability at the core at the core of the Strategic Plan, both through our programming strategies that are all aimed at building national and local ownership, but also through our revamped partnerships approach, with focus on working with and through others and building capacity of our partners. In terms of enhanced focus, we have simplified the results framework, going from the from 7 strategic plan outcomes in the previous cycle to 3, and also introduced fewer indicators so that we can measure our aggregate impact more clearly. Improving how we are actually telling our results story. I hope you all have visited our transparency portal, and if you haven't, please do so immediately after this session. We are in the process— Exactly. We are very proud of the Transparency Portal, and actually we are improving it further. Currently, we are publishing results and financial data against a strategic plan and strategic notes of the country offices and regional offices. But we will also in the future, later this year, publish results and financial data against projects, against the strategic note direct funding modality, and joint programmes later this year. So this, we believe, will help us to tell an even more powerful results story, including the impact of flexible and core funding. There was also a question on what were the lessons learned from the previous cycle that informed the current Strategic Plan. The key lessons learned from our work is that most effective and sustainable results come from adaptive evidence-based programming, which is locally owned, institutionally embedded, inclusive, and supported by strong monitoring and diversified funding. These lessons from the implementation of the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan were really central to the design of the current Strategic Plan. In terms of— there was also a request or sort of comment on the importance of monitoring the impact of our work. We have introduced a quarterly business review a few years ago, which is a very, very powerful internal tool which we have used so far to track the organizational efficiency and effectiveness results. Now, we are under the leadership of Nara Zai, we are introducing a standardized periodic development results monitoring as well. So this strengthens our monitoring, and it also helps us with— through our new results management system, PRISM, to really bring a focus on strategic-level monitoring for multi-year, whole strategic plan, and strategic note results. And just the last word on our strategic note process, so which covers all country and regional offices and all headquarters divisions. We are very important— we are very consistent in calling that we are clear not only on what results we want to be delivered, but also how we are delivering those, including by leveraging partnerships and our UN coordination mandate. But it is also important, I think all of us to recognize that strengthening capacity of partners and of the UN system as a whole takes time. I think we see this as a gradual process. It takes time before we can really measure results at the impact level. So let me just stop there in the interest of time, but I really want to thank you for your very insightful questions. We are happy to provide more details. Our leadership The whole leadership team is here on the podium and available in the course of the day. But again, really sincere thanks for your support and commitment to our mandate. Over to Nelson.

I thank the DED, Madame Kissi Madi, and I'll give the floor to the ED. The Director of the— Sorry. I give the floor to the DED, Deputy Executive Director, Madam Nyaradzaye Gumbo-Zivanda, you have the floor.

Thank you. Thank you so much, Mr. President. Let me join my Executive Director in her report and the responses also provided by Deputy Executive Director Kesi Made in reflecting on a number of key points on the issues that you have raised. First is a deep appreciation of the work that is happening in your own countries, an appreciation of a reaffirmation of our current strategic plan 2026 to 2029 and its four priorities, which really echoed the ethos of the United Nations Charter to ensure that we balance the peace and security agenda, the human rights focus, and development, respecting the humanitarian context within which we are— in the crisis context within which we respond. You raised and shared with us a very clear direction around impact, country ownership, country leadership, and that for us is where we are so much rooted within our coordination mandate, and how our strategic plans for the country, strategic notes, really aligns with the cooperation frameworks that are at the country level. We will share more information on the agenda that is before the board when we discuss our contribution to the sustainable development system, so we'll provide more details on the issues and the questions that you have raised. And equally, later this afternoon, you also have a discussion around the UN 18. Within that is also the groundedness of our involvement as UN Women on the country and regional research as a core of the reflections that you have raised. You also shared with us, and very deeply, around the Women, Peace and Security. Let me take this opportunity to congratulate the member states that at this moment we have 119 member states with national action plans on women, peace, and security. And that is member states— member states continue to lead in advancing the women, peace, and security, whether it's the focal points network or it's the Women, Peace, and Humanitarian Fund or the ELSI Initiative. It is the partners, the member states themselves who are leading this work and us— trusting us as UN Women to be your secretariat and to deliver together with other UN agencies. So with this peacebuilding work, we just wanted to reaffirm that. There were two other questions that I just want to do a quick reflection, conscious of time indeed. The lessons learnt. So one lesson— two lessons that we learnt is focus., and that focus is provided in the strategic plan that you adopted, which has only 3 systemic outcomes to ensure that we have a deep focus on the policies, laws, and norms which member states themselves develop, the focus on capacity and institutions— of institutions, and monitoring through data and resources, and the importance of communities and the rights holders. This, for us, is where the focus is within the context of the theme. Also, the clear commitment we have expressed throughout this discussion on young people, on young women and girls, we are deepening that work and we'll come back to you with the approaches that we are taking. The trust funds, which you also shared, which you contribute to, and which you co-lead, are a critical mechanism, especially at this moment of limited resources. That complements the support that you provide through assessed contributions and co-funding to make sure that we reach the communities and directly. I also want to appreciate the contribution, and especially from Finland, the echo on disability. The work on women, gender equality, and disability remains very important. I can attest to it in my own personal life, but really I just wanted to express our appreciation to it. We'll come back indeed within the course of the board's agenda to discuss more on coordination and how we are positioning our coordination work and our normative work as we prepare for CSW71, which should be focusing on the Sustainable Development Goals. So thank you so much, Mr. President, and I sit back your chair.
Thank you. I thank the Deputy Executive Director, Madam Nyara Dizayi, for her comments. I now give the floor to the ED, Madam Sima Bahaus. You have the floor.

Thank you. Thank you very much, our dear President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, and colleagues. Let me begin by expressing my sincere thanks and appreciation also to all of you delegates, to all of you who are in this room, for your very strong support to UN Women and to the work that we are doing together with you. We have heard you very clearly and we are very happy to hear what you have said this morning. I know that UN Women team in this room and equally our colleagues who are working every day across the globe in countries and regions we serve. They take great pride in the results we have achieved together. They are truly deserving of the recognition and the appreciation that you have expressed here today, and I must say that I am profoundly grateful to all of them for their dedication and hard work. It remains always my privilege to lead UN Women at this critical moment. Looking ahead, our focus across the organization is clear. We will continue to deliver on the Strategic Plan that you have approved in September. It remains our North Star, and we firmly believe it is the vehicle through which we can accelerate progress on sustainable development as well as on peace and security. We will pursue this with our unwavering commitment and dedication. Our work will continue to be guided by you and also by national priorities. We will work in close partnership with you, with civil society, and with women and girls in their diversity to deliver on our shared objectives. I really very much appreciate your strong— call for more flexible and predictable funding. Let me reiterate, this is the surest way for us to achieve our common goals. I thank you for underscoring this point, many of you did, and I ask you once again to take this message back to your capitals. We will be issuing our regular resources report next month, in line with your requests. And we will continue to strengthen our communication on results and on the return on investment in gender equality and women's empowerment. Excellencies, I have also heard the many views shared on the UNAID reform process, including the assessment of a potential merger between UN Women and UNFPA, and I look forward to discussing this further with you this afternoon. In this context, we will be guided by two central principles. First and foremost, delivering for all women and girls through a strong UN gender equality and women empowerment architecture. And second, by the decisions you as member states take. Across the broader reform agenda, UN Women will continue to leverage its coordination mandate, working closely with the resident coordinator system to strengthen coherence and impact at country level in support of gender equality and women's empowerment. Allow me to thank you once more for your guidance, for your trust, and for your confidence. This relationship we have with you, our Board, is among our most cherished, a space of deep commitment to women's rights, to women's empowerment, of support in advancing UN Women's triple mandate and of support to deliver lasting impact for all women and girls, to deliver on the promise of gender equality for everyone, for every woman and girl everywhere. I thank you and I look forward to seeing you this afternoon. Thank you.
